Description
The International Wolf Center is seeking applicants for the 2027 Dr. L. David Mech fellowship. As an investment in the future of wolf research and science-based wolf education, the Center awards up to two fellowships each year to undergraduate students or recent graduates interested in pursuing careers in natural sciences with an interest in wildlife. Fellowship recipients receive a $6,000 stipend and up to $4,000 in support for field research expenses.

Fellowship Goals
Reduce barriers to allow undergraduate students and recent graduates to directly engage in research and field work.
Encourage students from diverse backgrounds to explore natural sciences/wildlife biology as a profession.
Provide bridge support for early-career researchers prior to graduate school.

Fellowship Award Details
Application opens: November 1, 2026
Application deadline:  February 1, 2027
Fellowships Awarded: March 31, 2027
Term: April 1, 2027 through April 1, 2028
Stipend: $6,000
Research Allowance: up to $4,000 per year

Stipends are meant to support study and research during the tenure of the fellowship. Fellowship recipients are not employees, contracted workers, volunteers or interns of the International Wolf Center and are not covered by IWC’s benefits or insurance. All funds provided, including stipends and research allowances, are subject to tax. Fellows awarded stipends receive a financial summary at the end of each calendar year and are responsible for meeting their own state and federal tax obligations.

Research allowances are for equipment, supplies, research-related travel costs, housing, and other support required to participate in the project. A budget and general justification for these expenses must be included with your application.

A selection team of International Wolf Center staff and board review application materials and select recipients.

Eligibility
Applicant must be a U.S. citizen
Applicants must be either an upper-level student currently enrolled in an undergraduate institution or recently graduated within two years with an undergraduate degree.
Current graduate students, those accepted to graduate school and those already with graduate-level degrees in wildlife biology or a related field are not eligible.

Application Materials:
Purpose Statement: 500-800-word essay focusing on (a) why you are a good candidate through discussion of need for wildlife research experience, financial support and barriers you have faced, (b) your previous career-building experiences and future goals, (c) how you will accomplish the goals of the fellowship program, and (d) your project preference and ability to carry out the project work. Special consideration will be given to Black, Indigenous, and People of Color candidates.
Resume/CV
Budget Proposal: Include financial needs for support during the project. For reference, please see the Sample Budget Proposal. Estimated dollar amounts preferred but not required. You may enlist the help of the research lead to determine needs. If specific expenses are unknown at the time of application, please indicate this in lieu of a budget.
Project Selection: Selection of your preferred project from the provided list.
Reference Letter: An academic or professional reference letter referencing the applicants preferred project and ability to successfully complete the project, emailed by the reference to [email removed] before February 1, 2027.

Application Available At: https://wolf.org/programs/mech-fellowship/

Description
Request for Proposals (RFP) 

Appalachian Headwaters: 2027Graduate Student Field Research Grant 

1. Purpose and Overview 
Appalachian Headwaters invites proposals from master’s or PhD degree seeking students in environmental science, wildlife management, forestry, ecology, natural resource management, geography, or related fields to conduct field-based research in the Central Appalachian region. 
 
To strengthen the connection between academic research and applied restoration, all projects must include at least some components of field research conducted on Appalachian Headwaters property in Greenbrier County, West Virginia. 

2. Organizational Background 
Appalachian Headwaters is a nonprofit based in Lewisburg, WV, dedicated to environmental education and ecological restoration (https://appheadwaters.org/). Major initiatives include: 

Habitat restoration, wildlife, and pollinator garden programs 
Reforestation of degraded pastureland 
A native plant nursery supporting pollinator habitat and restoration plantings 
Environmental education programs for K–12 students and the public 
Citizen science program using wildlife cameras 
Research conducted through this grant program will directly support and expand on one or more of these initiatives.  

3. Appalachian Headwaters Properties 
Research supported through this grant must include a field component on Appalachian Headwaters’ property. Sites include: 

Wood Thrush Park: Mixed use property with educational facilities, trails, gardens, and restoration sites on approximately 150 acres. 
Kestrel Woods: Farmland Restoration Tract: More than 800-acre property, consisting of a 90-acre reforestation project and 750 acres of forest, including early successional to mature (>150-year-old) stands. 
Native Plant Nursery: Native plant propagation facility, producing pollinator-focused species and plants for retail and restoration projects, on approximately 60 acres of old pasture and secondary forest. 

Applicants should propose how research could incorporate one or more of these sites. Final site access and research design will be refined in partnership with Appalachian Headwaters staff if a proposal is selected for funding. 

4. Eligibility Criteria 

Enrollment in a master’s degree or PhD program at an accredited university. 
Relevant fields of study: environmental science, forestry, wildlife management, ecology, geography, or related discipline. 
Work must be conducted in the Appalachian region, with at least part of the research taking place on an Appalachian Headwaters property. 
Faculty advisor endorsement confirming academic standing and project feasibility. 
5. Funding Details 

Award Amount: Up to $3,000 per project 
Number of Awards: Up to 2 applicants per cycle, preference is given to first time applicants 
Funding Period: April–December 2026 
Allowable Expenses: Field equipment, research supplies, travel, data analysis, and community engagement. Tuition and general living expenses are not eligible. *Lodging provided on site, free of charge, at Wood Thrush Park. 
6. Research Focus Areas 

Priority will be given to projects that: 

Utilize Headwaters existing wildlife camera trap and/or invasive plant data sets 
Investigate pollinator biology, native plant ecology, or habitat management on Appalachian Headwaters’ properties. 
Contribute to ongoing research of the wildlife of Central Appalachia, including habitat use, genetics, survival, movement, and other monitoring initiatives  
Advance understanding of forest and watershed restoration on degraded agricultural landscapes. 
Examine ecological or hydrological processes tied to reforestation, invasive species management, or biodiversity. 
Include a community or educational engagement component. 
7. Proposal Components (12 pages max) 

Cover Page – Name, institution, program, advisor, project title. 
Abstract – ~300 words. 
Project Narrative – Background, objectives, methodology, significance, expected outcomes. 
Site Component – Description of how Headwaters’ property will be used as part of the research. Applicants may identify a preferred site type (e.g., forest, pollinator meadow, nursery). Final details will be refined in collaboration with Appalachian Headwaters staff if awarded. 
Timeline – Anticipated schedule of activities. 
Budget Justification – General breakdown of expenses. 
Applicant CV – 2 pages max. 
Faculty Advisor Letter – Statement of support and feasibility. 

8. Review Criteria 
Scientific Merit – Strength of research design and objectives. 
Alignment with Mission – Relevance to Appalachian Headwaters’ restoration and education goals. 
Use of Headwaters’ Property – Clear integration of Appalachian Headwaters’ land into research activities. 
Feasibility – Realistic timeline and budget. 
Community/Educational Impact – Potential to involve or benefit local communities. 

9. Submission Process 

Deadline: Friday, January 31, 2027 (11:59 PM ET) 
Submission: Apply at this link by filling out the application and attaching your Proposal as a PDF. No submissions via email please. If you have questions, you can reach out to Dr. Merri Collins at [email removed] 
Notification of selection: Early March 2026 
Start of Funding: April 2026 

10. Reporting Requirements 
Awardees must:
Deliver a final report (5–10 pages) summarizing findings and relevance to Appalachian Headwaters programs. 
Provide a public-accessible resource (e.g., StoryMap, public talk, community workshop). 
Acknowledge Appalachian Headwaters in academic presentations and publications. 

11. Past Recipients 
Elizabeth Kramer: PhD Student at Ohio University. 2026. “Phylogeography, hybridization, and species delimitation in a complex of cryptic woodland salamanders in central Appalachia.” 
Brian Brillhart: Masters Student at Marshall University. 2026. “Analysis of Black-capped (Poecile atricapillus) and Carolina Chickadee (P. carolinensis) Vocalizations in Allopatric vs. Sympatric Populations.” 
Contact
Dr. Merri Collins
[email removed] (preferred contact method)

Description
 *Applications are reviewed on a rolling-basis and applications may close before the deadline.

ARS Office/Lab and Location: A postdoctoral research opportunity is currently available with the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), Agricultural Research Service (ARS), Environmental Microbial and Food Safety Laboratory. The appointment may be based at either the Beltsville Agricultural Research Center (BARC) in Beltsville, Maryland, or the Eastern Regional Research Center (ERRC) in Wyndmoor, Pennsylvania.

The Agricultural Research Service (ARS) is the U.S. Department of Agriculture's chief scientific in-house research agency with a mission to find solutions to agricultural problems that affect Americans every day from field to table. ARS will deliver cutting-edge, scientific tools and innovative solutions for American farmers, producers, industry, and communities to support the nourishment and well-being of all people; sustain our nation’s agroecosystems and natural resources; and ensure the economic competitiveness and excellence of our agriculture. The vision of the agency is to provide global leadership in agricultural discoveries through scientific excellence.

Research Project: This project focuses on developing optical sensing and artificial intelligence (AI) methods for food safety inspection. Research will integrate sensing with machine learning and deep learning to investigate relationships between optical measurements and food safety attributes. Applications include rapid identification of foodborne bacteria (e.g., E. coli, Listeria, and Salmonella) and detection of mycotoxin contamination in food and agricultural products (e.g., aflatoxin in corn).

Under the guidance of USDA-ARS scientists, you may assist in experimental design and collecting and analyzing data using various imaging and spectroscopy techniques, such as reflectance, fluorescence, Raman, color, transmission, hyperspectral, and multispectral. Research activities may include helping in the development and improvement of sensing systems and control software, image and spectral processing, multimodal data fusion, and development of AI models for detection, classification, and prediction. You may collaborate with researchers in engineering, microbiology, and chemistry to help investigate sensing approaches for food safety applications. Participation may also assist in preparation of scientific manuscripts and conference presentations. These activities will provide hands-on research experience that complements your background. 

Learning Objectives: Under the guidance of a mentor, you will:

Learn and apply optical sensing techniques, including reflectance, fluorescence, Raman, color, transmission, hyperspectral, and multispectral, for identifying foodborne bacteria and detecting mycotoxin contamination in food and agricultural products.
Gain hands-on experience in design, development, and experimental evaluation of optical sensing instruments and prototype systems for rapid food safety inspection.
Develop skills in image and spectral processing, feature extraction, multimodal data fusion, and machine learning and deep learning, for food safety detection, classification, and prediction.
Strengthen interdisciplinary collaboration and scientific communication skills through assisting in research discussions, preparation of manuscripts for peer-reviewed journals, and presentation of findings at scientific conferences.
Mentor(s): The mentor for this opportunity is Jianwei Qin ([email removed]). If you have questions about the nature of the research, please contact the mentor(s).

Anticipated Appointment Start Date: 2026/2027. Start date is flexible and will depend on a variety of factors.

Appointment Length: The appointment will initially be for one year, but may be renewed upon recommendation of ARS and is contingent on the availability of funds.

Level of Participation: The appointment is full time.

Citizenship Requirements: This opportunity is available to U.S. citizens only.

ORISE Information: This program, administered by ORAU through its contract with the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) to manage the Oak Ridge Institute for Science and Education (ORISE), was established through an interagency agreement between DOE and ARS. Participants do not become employees of USDA, ARS, DOE or the program administrator, and there are no employment-related benefits. Proof of health insurance is required for participation in this program. Health insurance can be obtained through ORISE.

Questions: Please visit our Program Website. After reading, if you have additional questions about the application process, please email [email removed] and include the reference code for this opportunity.

Qualifications
Applicants should have received or be currently pursuing a doctoral degree in agricultural/biosystems engineering, mechanical engineering, electrical/computer engineering, computer science, food science, or a related field.

Preferred skills:

Experience with imaging and spectroscopy, such as reflectance, fluorescence, Raman, color, transmission, hyperspectral, and multispectral.
Experience with optical sensing instrumentation, laboratory automation, robotics, and LabVIEW programming for system control and integration.
Experience applying machine learning, deep learning, and chemometrics to image and spectral data, including preprocessing, feature extraction, data fusion, and model evaluation.
Proficiency in Python and MATLAB for scientific programming and data analysis.
Familiarity with AI frameworks (e.g., PyTorch or TensorFlow) and models (e.g., YOLO and ViT) is desirable.
Experience setting up computational environments and training and running AI models on GPU servers is also preferred.
Familiarity with food safety research, particularly identification of foodborne bacteria and detection and analysis of mycotoxins.
Strong experimental design, data analysis and interpretation, scientific writing, oral communication, and collaborative research skills.
Stipend
$80,000.00 – $110,000.00 Yearly
Point of Contact
Janeen

Citizenship: U.S. Citizen Only
Degree: Doctoral Degree.

Description
 *Applications are reviewed on a rolling-basis and applications may close before the deadline.

USGS Office/Lab and Location: A research opportunity is currently available with the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) located in Boulder, Colorado.

The USGS mission is to monitor, analyze, and predict current and evolving dynamics of complex human and natural Earth-system interactions and to deliver actionable intelligence at scales and timeframes relevant to decision makers. As the Nation's largest water, earth, and biological science and civilian mapping agency, USGS collects, monitors, analyzes, and provides science about natural resource conditions, issues, and problems. 

The USGS programs supporting this research—the Water Mission Area National Water Quality Program and the Ecosystems Mission Area Toxic Substances Hydrology Program— focus on supporting national-scale reconnaissance and prediction of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), harmful algal blooms (HABs), and associated toxins. Program goals emphasize targeted research and development to create advanced laboratory methods for detecting and documenting these emerging toxic threats. The programs also aim to advance understanding of the processes governing contaminant transport, persistence, natural attenuation, and geochemical transformation. Together, these efforts strengthen the scientific basis for forecasting the development, duration, and decline of emerging contaminants across environmental matrices to improve prediction and management.

Research Project: Microorganisms play an important role in the fate and transport of environmental contaminants through processes such as degradation, sorption, motility, and life-cycle dynamics. This fellowship will investigate how microbiological processes influence the environmental behavior of HABs and PFAS by identifying and quantifying the mechanisms through which harmful algal species govern sorption, release, and transformation of PFAS in aquatic systems. You will have the opportunity to develop laboratory methods to characterize biological drivers that shape contaminant movement, retention, bioavailability, and exposure within phytoplanktonic and benthic algal communities. This training provides exposure to interdisciplinary scientific approaches required to provide Federal, Tribal, and State partners with the data and tools needed for evidence-based decision making and natural-resource management.

Learning Objectives: This fellowship provides a unique educational opportunity where you will:

Collaborate with a supportive scientific community of interdisciplinary researchers across the USGS Ecosystem and Water Mission Areas. 
Design and implement laboratory experiments and apply advanced molecular biology and bioinformatics approaches to evaluate how environmental stressors influence contaminant fate with mentor guidance.
Gain hands-on experience integrating molecular technologies with microbial ecology and environmental chemistry.
Receive training on methods used to produce holistic ecological assessments such as field observation, laboratory experimentation, and computational analysis.
Strengthen scientific communication skills through the dissemination of research findings related to contaminant transport, ecosystem health, and decision-support frameworks for resource managers.
Mentor: The mentor for this opportunity is Jennifer Underwood ([email removed]). If you have questions about the nature of the research please contact the mentor(s). 

Anticipated Appointment Start Date: March 1, 2027. Start date is flexible and will depend on a variety of factors.

Appointment Length: The appointment will initially be for one year, but may be renewed upon recommendation of DOI and is contingent on the availability of funds.

Level of Participation: The appointment is full time.

Participant Stipend: Stipend rates may vary based on numerous factors, including opportunity, location, education, and experience. If you are interviewed, you can inquire about the exact stipend rate at that time and if selected, your appointment offer will include the monthly stipend rate.

Citizenship Requirements: This opportunity is available to U.S. citizens and Lawful Permanent Residents (LPR) only.

ORISE Information: This program, administered by ORAU through its contract with the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) to manage the Oak Ridge Institute for Science and Education (ORISE), was established through an interagency agreement between DOE and USGS. Participants do not become employees of USGS, DOE or the program administrator, and there are no employment-related benefits. Proof of health insurance is required for participation in this program. Health insurance can be obtained through ORISE.

Questions: If you have questions about the application process please email [email removed] and include the reference code for this opportunity.

Qualifications
The qualified candidate should be currently pursuing or have received a doctoral degree in one of the relevant fields.

Description
 Canada Excellence Research Chair (CERC) Dr. Deborah McGregor and the research program in Indigenous Planetary Well-being at the University of Calgary are seeking three highly motivated students to contribute to enriched understanding of Indigenous contributions to addressing environmental challenges. Selected applicants will be supported by our research team in applying for admission to the University of Calgary in either the Department of Geography, the Department of Earth, Energy, and the Environment, or the Transdisciplinary Graduate program, depending on specific project and student’s interest. Student will be based out of the University of Calgary, with significant field work with collaborators and partners in locations throughout Ontario and Alberta. 

Application: To apply, please send a CV and cover letter to Carina at [email removed]; applications are rolling with a preferred review deadline of November 20. Please indicate which of the three projects you are interested in and outline your interest and qualifications in your cover letter. 

Projects: 
1.        Indigenous Urban Climate Action, project will involve: 
• Contribute to an original and innovative research program that seeks to document the nature and impact of Indigenous climate action in cities and urban settings (e.g. document urban land stewardship practices) 
• Contribute to understanding how Indigenous climate action influence city and urban climate policy and governance 
• Contribute to an Indigenous urban climate assessment 
• Generate understanding of how Indigenous laws, rights and knowledge can accelerate climate action in cities and urban contexts 
• Generate understanding of the relationships between urban and rural Indigenous led climate action 
• Contribute to supporting Indigenous urban climate priorities 
• Indigenous research methods will be co-designed and produced and may involve: supporting and/or leading interviews; workshops; learning circles, and land-based engagement activities 
• Facilitating knowledge sharing and mobilization and leading community engagement activities and youth engagement activities 
• Contribute to knowledge mobilization activities (multi-media, videos) including organizing speaker series, webinars and workshops 

2.        Indigenous Planetary Well-being, project will involve: 
• Through a collaborative research process, seek to develop the concept of Indigenous planetary well-being 
• Co-develop Indigenous led and community-based well-being frameworks 
• Co-develop Indigenous led and community-based indicators that measure well being 
• Engage with Indigenous knowledge, language, rights, laws and values to develop original indicators of well-being 
• This research may involve leading interviews, workshops, learning circles, Indigenous and community-engaged research methods and land-based activities 
• Facilitate knowledge sharing and mobilization and lead community engagement activities, including with youth 
• Develop skills related to Indigenous research methodologies, knowledge mobilization, and community engagement 

3.        Indigenous Knowledge, Languages and Land-based Practices and Planetary Well-being, project will involve: 
• Advance the revitalization of Indigenous languages, knowledge, laws and land-based practices in support of community well being 
• Co-develop Indigenous led and community-based land-based activities that support the goals of community and planetary well being 
• Co-develop Indigenous led and community-based youth and multi-generational knowledge sharing gatherings 
• Support community led projects that support various aspects of planetary well-being. 
• In collaboration with Indigenous partners, convene Elders, TK holders/practitioners, and youth together to share priorities for future activities that strengthen and restore relationships to the Earth 
• Facilitate knowledge sharing and mobilization and lead community engagement activities, including with youth 
• Develop skills related to Indigenous research methodologies, knowledge mobilization, and community engagement 

Qualifications: 
• Indigenous cultural competency, with experience working with Indigenous communities and/or organizations 
• Undergraduate and/or master's degree in environmental science/studies, health, Indigenous studies, education, urban studies, or related fields 
• Experience with Indigenous research approaches and methodologies and/or community-engaged methods is an asset 
• Experience and skills in literature review and synthesis, writing, qualitative data analysis, and academic writing are assets 
• Excellent communication skills and an interest in knowledge sharing/mobilization 
• Experience coordinating multi-generational gatherings and working with youth are assets 

Contact
Carina Burroughs

Description
 Description 

I am seeking one highly motivated student to join my research group in the Department of Natural Resources and Environmental Sciences (NRES) at the University of Illinois Urbana Champaign. Start date will be mid-May 2027. 

During the summer of 2027, the student will analyze a long-term passive acoustic monitoring dataset to determine presence/absence for T & E bat species in National Park Service units in the Upper Midwest and visit the NPS units with Dr. O’Keefe to evaluate the available habitat. During the following academic year, the student will develop distribution models for T & E bats using habitat layers. At present, there is only one year of funding available but there is the potential for a second year of funding that would enable mistnetting surveys to validate GIS models. If the funding is not renewed, the student will be supported through teaching assistantships or fellowships during the second academic year. This study is funded by and will be conducted in collaboration with the National Park Service. Results will inform policy on conservation practices to enhance and protect habitat for federally endangered bats. 

Minimum Qualifications 

Applicants should have a BS degree in biology, ecology, wildlife, or another related discipline. Preferred qualifications include strong quantitative and analytical skills, field research experience, and a competitive GPA. Excellent writing and verbal communication skills, a strong work ethic, and the ability to both work independently and contribute to a research team will also be beneficial. A valid driver’s license is also required. 

Preferred Experience 

Experience with identifying bat calls, processing bat acoustic data in standard software packages, working with large amounts of data, and developing maps in GIS. 

How to Apply 

If interested, please send an email to Dr. Joy O’Keefe ([email removed]) by November 23, 2026 with the following combined into one PDF with your last name in the file name: CV, undergraduate transcripts (unofficial are sufficient), statement of interest addressing minimum qualifications and preferred experience for this project, and contact information for three references. 

Contact
Joy O'Keefe

Description
Drs. James Beasley, Travis DeVault, and Jessy Patterson are seeking three highly motivated students with strong academic credentials to join our team and pursue PhD degrees in wildlife ecology at the University of Georgia. Applicants must possess well-developed organizational skills and demonstrated excellence in written and oral communication. The successful applicants will enroll in the Warnell School of Forestry & Natural Resources in Summer (preferred) or Fall 2027. They will be stationed at the Savannah River Ecology Laboratory in Aiken, SC when not taking classes or collecting field data. 
 The successful applicants will join a large, interdisciplinary team focused on understanding and preventing damage by invasive wild pigs to agriculture, native species, and other natural resources throughout South Carolina. Student projects will focus on population dynamics, spatial ecology, agricultural and environmental damage assessments, and impacts of invasive wild pigs on native wildlife. Students will develop research questions within this framework to comprise their dissertations, depending on individual research interests. Students will work in close collaboration with other students, faculty, and agency personnel associated with this research. 
 Qualifications: Applicants must have completed an MS degree in wildlife biology, ecology, or a related discipline prior to enrolling at Warnell. Prior experience conducting ecological field work is required. Applicants should also have a demonstrated interest in resolving and understanding human-wildlife conflicts, excellent organizational, writing, and communication skills, and evidence of strong quantitative skills. Experience working with state and federal stakeholders as well as private landowners is preferred. 
 Application: Review of applications will begin immediately and will continue until suitable candidates are found. Applicants should submit a letter of interest, CV (including GPA and GRE scores, if available), and contact information for three references in a single pdf attachment to Dr. Jessy Patterson ([email removed]). Description
Summary: Seeking a motivated MS student to lead research on the breeding ecology of Eastern Bluebirds (Sialia sialis) at Arkansas Tech University. The project will utilize an established array of 120 Eastern Bluebird nest boxes, where the student will continue collecting data for long-term population monitoring while also developing new research questions using data unique to their project. Beyond this core monitoring, the specific research focus is somewhat flexible, and the student will be able to tailor it to match their interests. The faculty advisor (Dr. Doug Barron – https://douglasbarron.weebly.com/) has experience monitoring reproductive success of wild birds and using behavior, genetics, hormones, and disease monitoring to generate a more comprehensive understanding of avian ecology. The student will be encouraged to incorporate some combination of these approaches to develop a multidisciplinary thesis.
 This research will be the focus of the student’s thesis for a Master of Science in Fisheries and Wildlife Science at Arkansas Tech University. ATU is the third-largest university in the state, with an enrollment of approximately 10,000 students. The Russellville campus, located in the scenic Arkansas River Valley between the Ozark and Ouachita Mountains, is about an hour from the capital city of Little Rock and boasts a charming blend of historic and modern architecture, including beautiful grounds and green spaces. For more information about the Fisheries and Wildlife Science program and the MS degree, visit https://www.atu.edu/programs/?id=fisheries-wildlife-science-ms.
 Salary: This year-round position is supported by a teaching assistantship that includes a full tuition waiver and a stipend of $14,000 per year. Teaching duties occur during the fall and spring semesters only; summers are dedicated to field research. Beyond assistantship duties, the student is expected to devote full-time effort to coursework and thesis research. The position is expected to last for 2.5 years, contingent on satisfactory performance and academic progress. 
 Start Date: Between January 1–11, 2027. 
 Qualifications: Applicants must meet the requirements of the Graduate College and have completed a bachelor’s degree in biology, wildlife science, or a related field by the start date. Applicants must also have a good driving record (capable of operating a state vehicle) and must pass a background check. 
 The ideal candidate will exhibit a passion for avian ecology and will have experience with associated field techniques. Comfort with basic laboratory techniques and experience with genetic or physiological assays are a plus but are not required; lab skills can be taught to a student who is willing to learn.
 Required:
·         BS in Biology, Fisheries and Wildlife, or related field
 Preferred Field Experience (in order of importance):
·         One year of field experience
·         Mist netting and bird banding
·         Ornithology coursework
·         Nest searching and/or monitoring
 Preferred Laboratory Experience (in order of importance):
·         Basic laboratory techniques (e.g., pipetting, use of lab equipment)
·         Genetics, endocrinology, entomology, or disease ecology coursework
·         Conducting lab assays (e.g., PCR, EIA)
 Application Process: Applications will be reviewed as they are received, and the position will be filled once a qualified candidate is selected. Applicants are encouraged to apply promptly to ensure consideration.
 To apply, send a single PDF file that includes: 1) cover letter detailing your interest, qualifications, and available start date, 2) resume/CV, 3) unofficial transcripts, and 4) contact information for three professional references.
 Email materials to Dr. Doug Barron at [email removed] with the subject line “Eastern Bluebird MS Assistantship.”
Contact
Doug Barron
[email removed] (preferred contact method)

Description
OPEN POSITION:
Fully funded M.S. assistantship in grazing systems ecology

Salary: $36,000 + health insurance

Anticipated Start Date: Summer 2027
(Applications will be accepted until a suitable candidate is identified)

Offered by:
Texas A&M University Center for Grazinglands and Ranch Management
Research Fields: Range and pasture assessment/fecal diet quality

Description:
The Texas A&M University Center for Grazinglands and Ranch Management (CGRM) is seeking applications for a Master’s of Science student who will work with Dr. Jeff Goodwin and research team on a fully funded project to conduct baseline ecological assessments on 20 ranches across Texas. Baseline assessments will include rangeland health or pasture condition scoring and fecal sample collection to determine diet quality using near infrared reflectance spectroscopy (NIRS) technology. The successful candidate will also be responsible for comparing livestock performance nutritional prediction models. The Texas A&M Center for Grazinglands and Ranch Management aims to safeguard the ecologic and economic resiliency of grazingland resources and ranching operations with a focus on producer-directed, applied grazingland and ranch management research, outreach and engagement. CGRM develops and supports interdisciplinary collaborations to address critical needs in the ranching community and strives to achieve three overarching goals: enhance operational resiliency, strengthen enterprise sustainability, and foster the future of the industry. Texas A&M University (TAMU) is a public, land-grant institution dedicated to the discovery, development, communication, and application of knowledge in a wide range of academic and professional fields. Its high-quality graduate programs prepare students to assume roles in leadership and service to society, and seeks to serve people of all racial, ethnic, and geographic groups as it addresses the needs of an increasingly diverse population and global economy. Texas A&M Agrilife Research pioneers knowledge about agriculture and natural resources to enhance agricultural and ecological systems and develop sustainable production systems.

Responsibilities:
Responsibilities will include conducting baseline rangeland health evaluations and/or pasture condition scoring on ranches across diverse ecological regions in Texas. The goal of this component is to establish baseline conditions of plant productivity and health,
plant structure and composition, and soil erosion and soil health resource concerns. Additionally, the successful candidate will be responsible for collecting fecal samples from participating ranches to conduct fecal diet quality analysis using NIRS and compare alternative nutritional models that predict livestock performance and make supplementation recommendations.

REQUIRED QUALIFICATIONS:
- B.S. in rangeland management, animal science, natural resources management, ecosystem management or closely related field
- GPA of 3.0 or greater
- Strong work ethic and self-motivated
- Valid U.S. driver’s license

PREFERRED QUALIFICATIONS:
- Knowledge or experience conducting field work on ranches
- Experience working effectively with livestock producers
- Experience or working knowledge of beef cattle operations and management strategies
- Excellent oral communication and technical writing skills

HOW TO APPLY

Applicants should email:
1) A statement of interest (2 pages maximum)
2) Undergraduate and graduate transcripts (unofficial versions accepted)
3) A resume or CV, and
4) Names, phone numbers, and e-mail addresses for three references
To: Dr. Jeff Goodwin at [email removed] with the subject line ‘GLCI Ranchworthy MS Position’
Review of applications will begin immediately and will continue until the position is filled. Contact Dr. Goodwin ([email removed]) for more information.
Contact
Dr. Jeff Goodwin
[email removed] (preferred contact method)

Offered by: Texas A&M University Center for Grazinglands and Ranch Management

Research Fields: Range and pasture assessment, mealybug infestation and remediation

Description:
The Texas A&M University Center for Grazinglands and Ranch Management (CGRM) is seeking applications for a Master of Science student who will work with Dr. Jeff Goodwin and a team of researchers on a fully funded project to conduct baseline ecological assessments on ranches in Texas. Baseline assessments will include rangeland health or pasture condition scoring, including species composition and bare ground percentages. The successful candidate will also be responsible for quantifying mealybug infestation levels, participating in producer interviews, and assisting with demonstration sites.

The pasture mealybugs (Heliococcus summervillei and H. novovillei) have emerged as one of the most significant new threats to Texas grazinglands, with confirmed infestations in 114 counties with additional counties considered at imminent risk. The pest threatens more than 20 million acres of Texas pasture and rangeland, causing forage losses ranging from 30 to 50 percent and, in some cases, complete pasture failure. As the pest continues to spread across the southern United States, Texas livestock producers face declining forage productivity, increased supplemental feeding costs, reduced carrying capacity, and costly pasture renovation. The Texas A&M Center for Grazinglands and Ranch Management aims to safeguard the ecological and economic resiliency of grazingland resources and ranching operations with a focus on producer-directed, applied grazingland and ranch management research, outreach and engagement. CGRM develops and supports interdisciplinary collaborations to address critical needs in the ranching community and strives to achieve three overarching goals: enhance operational resiliency, strengthen enterprise sustainability, and foster the future of the industry. Texas A&M University (TAMU) is a public, land-grant institution dedicated to the discovery, development, communication, and application of knowledge in a wide range of academic and professional fields. Its high-quality graduate programs prepare students to assume roles in leadership and service to society, and it seeks to serve people of all racial, ethnic, and geographic groups as it addresses the needs of an increasingly diverse population and
global economy. Texas A&M AgriLife Research pioneers knowledge about agriculture and natural resources to enhance agricultural and ecological systems and develop sustainable production systems.

Responsibilities:
Baseline Resource and Grazinglands Health assessments will focus on plant species composition, level of mealybug infestation, pasture condition scores, rangeland health scores, and producer interviews to determine perceptions of species susceptibility and management history. Information obtained from interviews will help guide ongoing investigation and demonstration to identify most effective strategies for mitigation and management. Species composition and level of infestation baselines will help determine how level of infestation changes across grass species. Individual species' susceptibility to mealybugs is currently unknown. Assessments will be conducted on individual Texas operations distributed across South Texas, Central Texas, and the Gulf Coast Prairie.

REQUIRED QUALIFICATIONS:
- B.S. in rangeland management, natural resources management, ecosystem management or closely related field
- GPA of 3.0 or greater
- Strong work ethic and self-motivated
- Valid U.S. driver’s license

PREFERRED QUALIFICATIONS:
- Knowledge or experience conducting field data collection on ranches
- Experience working directly with livestock producers
- Experience or working knowledge of rangeland management strategies
- Excellent oral communication and technical writing skills

Applicants should email:
1) A statement of interest (2 pages maximum)
2) Undergraduate and graduate transcripts (unofficial versions accepted)
3) A resume or CV, and
4) Names, phone numbers, and e-mail addresses for three references
To: Dr. Jeff Goodwin at [email removed] with the subject line ‘GLCI Mealybug MS Position’
Review of applications will begin immediately and will continue until the position is filled. Contact Dr. Goodwin ([email removed]) for more information.

Description
A PhD studentship is available with Dr. Mitch Weegman in the Department of Biology at the University of Saskatchewan (https://www.ducks.ca/our-work/science/saskatchewan-endowed-chair/). The student will lead a research project on the population ecology of Greenland white-fronted geese, using 40-year data sets to address long-standing questions about drivers of productivity on breeding areas and subpopulation structure. 
 The Greenland white-fronted goose population has continued to decline, from a peak of 35,000 individuals in 1999 to 13,000 individuals in 2025. Productivity is the proximate mechanism for population change and there is continued uncertainty about the degree to which breeding conditions explain variation in productivity. Further, there are ~45 wintering Greenland white-fronted goose flocks (subpopulations) with hypothesized differential demographic structure contributing to the decline and winter range contraction. This PhD studentship has been developed to encourage discovery with anticipated conservation application. Our project goals are to (1) estimate the environmental drivers on breeding areas of productivity in Greenland white-fronted geese, (2) identify structure in survival and reproductive success among 45 wintering Greenland white-fronted goose flocks, and (3) connect population and individual processes linking demography with individual movement and behaviour. The student will use data from thousands of neck-collared individuals and hundreds of GPS-tagged individuals spanning 40 years. This project is an international partnership among National Parks and Wildlife Service (Ireland), Aarhus University (Denmark) and University of Saskatchewan (Canada). There will be substantial additional opportunities for the student to collaborate on other projects in population and movement ecology.
 Prerequisites: Ideal candidates will have an MSc and undergraduate degree in ecology, statistics or a closely related field, and interpersonal skills to lead discussions among collaborators. Preference will be given to those with a strong quantitative background (e.g., experience with Program R, Bayesian methods) and knowledge of migratory bird ecology and management. Students must have a valid driver’s license. The successful applicant will be expected to publish manuscripts in peer-reviewed journals and present papers at scientific meetings.
 Salary and benefits: $35,000 Canadian per year plus compensation for tuition and fees
 Start date: 1 May or 1 September 2027
 Last date to apply: 30 November 2026 
 To be considered for this position, please send the following (preferably as a single PDF) to Dr. Mitch Weegman ([email removed]):
 (1) Letter of interest summarizing your experience, (2) Curriculum vitae or resume, (3) University transcripts (unofficial are OK), (4) Contact information for three references.

Description
Graduate Student Opportunities in Urban Animal Cognition and Behavior

Dr. Lauren Stanton | Department of Biological Sciences | Illinois State University
Our research group investigates how animals perceive, learn about, and respond to the challenges and opportunities of living in human-altered environments. We are particularly interested in how individual differences shape wildlife responses to urbanization, influence human-wildlife interactions, and inform coexistence strategies. Looking forward, we will explore how early life experiences, social learning, and cultural transmission further shape animal behavior within and across cities. 

We value partnerships with local communities and recognize community science and public engagement as necessary for not only understanding urban wildlife, but also for the development of effective, equitable approaches to human-wildlife coexistence.


Current Research Opportunities
Graduate students will contribute to an ongoing research program investigating the behavior and ecology of urban raccoons (Procyon lotor) in San Francisco, California. This Bay Area Raccoon Project includes a substantial existing dataset, providing opportunities to investigate questions related to urban animal physiology, health, behavior, cognition, social interactions, movement, and space use.

MS Student (1 position)
The MS student will primarily use existing GPS and biologging data from the Bay Area Raccoon Project for their thesis chapters. This position is particularly well suited to someone interested in asking novel questions by integrating behavioral, animal telemetry, and geospatial datasets.

Potential research topics include individual- and neighborhood-level differences in raccoon activity, health, and risk-taking behavior. The student will work closely with existing collaborators to develop focused, independent research questions using available data. 

Previous research or field experience is expected (see more below). Basic familiarity with R and statistical analyses is required. Additional experience with data analysis, GIS, writing, or science communication is highly desirable. 

 
PhD Student (1 position)
The PhD student will contribute to the existing Bay Area Raccoon Project as part of their dissertation (1–2 chapters), while also developing new, independent investigations (2–3 additional chapters).

Experimental investigations will likely involve additional fieldwork and data collection with raccoons in San Francisco, although opportunities to develop complementary research in Illinois, or with other species, may also be possible. The student will have substantial opportunities to develop independent research questions and pursue work at the intersection of animal behavior, cognition, urban ecology, and human-wildlife interactions.

Experience developing hypotheses, conducting independent research, analyzing data, and communicating findings through presentations or publications is expected. Proficiency in R and experience with statistical analyses are strongly preferred. A publication, manuscript in preparation, or other evidence of research productivity is highly desirable. See below for additional details.

 Who Should Apply?
We are looking for motivated, creative, and collaborative students with demonstrated experience working in research or applied animal settings. Competitive applicants will have some combination of the following:

Research interests: A strong interest in animal cognition, as well as wildlife behavior, movement ecology, urban ecology, and conservation biology.
Research experience: Previous experience in an academic research laboratory, field research project, or a related setting.
Animal experience: Experience working with animals in a field, zoo, wildlife rehabilitation center, veterinary clinic, or similar professional setting.
Quantitative skills: Basic knowledge of R and statistics, with some understanding of multivariate analyses. Experience or interest in developing skills in machine learning, GIS/spatial analyses, and computational approaches to classifying animal behavior from biologging data is highly desirable.
Communication: Strong written, verbal, and interpersonal skills, with the ability to communicate effectively with both academic and non-academic audiences (e.g., when engaging with the public). Organizational and leadership skills are also desirable. We especially value individuals who are enthusiastic, collaborative, and bring curiosity to their work.
 

How to Apply
Interested applicants should email Dr. Lauren Stanton at [email removed] with the following materials in a single PDF file labeled with the applicant’s last name:

A CV or resume.
A brief statement describing their research interests, relevant experience, quantitative skills, and reasons for wanting to join the lab. Please indicate whether you are applying for the MS or PhD position.
Contact information for 3 references.

Please state “Application for ISU graduate position” in the email subject line

Application review will begin immediately, and selected candidates will formally apply to the graduate program by February 1, 2027. Additional information about graduate studies at Illinois State University can be found here: https://illinoisstate.edu/academics/graduate

Lauren Stanton

---

Two MS Graduate Research Assistantships are available starting May 2026 in the PEASE Lab (peaselab.com) at Southern Illinois University to continue our statewide wild turkey (Meleagris gallopavo) ecology and management project. One student will lead efforts on gobbling chronology, and the other student will lead efforts on nesting phenology. The students will be co-advised by Drs. Brent Pease and Guillaume Bastille-Rousseau at Southern Illinois University.

One student will focus on wild turkey gobbling chronology. The student will lead field efforts using autonomous recording units (ARUs) to document spatial and/or temporal variation in gobbling chronology (e.g., Kreh et al., 2023 Wildlife Society Bulletin). The focus of this research is to assess timing of male gobbling across Illinois to determine whether current spring harvest season regulations (e.g., timing, zoning, and length of spring harvest seasons) are aligned with timing of gobbling and then provide regulatory recommendations. Addition work will focus on identifying environmental drivers of variation in gobbling chronology as well as methodological work in ARUs, species identification from audio recordings, and/or continued ongoing work within our lab on population estimation (e.g., abundance) via ARU recordings.

One student will focus on wild turkey nesting phenology. The student will lead trapping efforts to tag hens with GPS transmitters to document spatial and/or temporal variation in nesting phenology as well as spatial ecology of turkeys in southern Illinois. Primary field duties include capture and affixing GPS radiotags, monitoring hen survival and nesting and brooding success, and identifying local and landscape factors contributing to movement patterns. Research will emphasize general spatial ecology and population ecology (e.g., movement, space-use, survival, etc.).

This is a well-funded, multi-agency research project, and the graduate students will be expected to assist in hiring and managing field technicians to support the data collection efforts. Additionally, although research questions will be unique among the selected students, their field work will be complimentary, and all individuals will be expected to contribute to all wild turkey research activities carried out. The successful applicants will have (1) obtained B.S. degree in wildlife, ecology, biology, forestry, zoology, or related fields; (2) knowledge of wild turkey ecology; (3) interest in developing quantitative skills with experience using a variety of data types and models; (4) interest in developing knowledge of program R and spatial software (e.g., QGIS, ArcGIS); (5) a driver's license and ability to conduct independent field work in difficult conditions (e.g., steep terrain, poison ivy, ticks); (6) strong oral and written communication skills, and (7) a cooperative, team-oriented mindset eager to carry out wildlife research and address key problems in wildlife conservation and management.

Please see the PEASE lab website (https://peaselab.com/) and the SIU Forestry Program’s homepage (https://forestry.siu.edu) for more information on our research and academic department.

Description
Great Hollow Nature Preserve & Ecological Research Center is pleased to announce the opening of a two-year, open-topic fellowship to support a post-doctoral scientist at our preserve in New Fairfield, Connecticut. The Fellow will: (1) design and conduct independent research at Great Hollow and/or other appropriate study sites in the region, (2) assist with other research projects of Great Hollow’s, (3) help coordinate and mentor Great Hollow’s summer interns, and (4) contribute to the general day-to-day operation of Great Hollow as a member of our small staff, including but not limited to occasional assistance with outreach, community events, and land management. The ideal candidate will be an ecologist whose research is field-based, integrative, and innovative, has a conservation application, and will complement or add to Great Hollow’s active areas of study. Candidates may work on any taxa and in any subdiscipline that is relevant to the biodiversity and ecological communities of the northeastern U.S., although animal ecologists will likely be the most competitive.  The fellowship is intended for early career scientists who have completed their PhD within the past 5 years. PhD candidates who expect to defend during the spring of 2027 and who meet all other qualifications below are also eligible to apply.

About Great Hollow

Founded in 2016, Great Hollow is a non-profit environmental education and research center located in New Fairfield, Connecticut, a little more than an hour north of New York City. Great Hollow is dedicated to the advancement of biodiversity conservation, applied ecological research, and experiential environmental education in Connecticut and beyond.  Our 825-acre preserve is contiguous or nearly contiguous with thousands of acres of additional protected land in Connecticut and neighboring New York State. The preserve is also near Candlewood Lake, which is the largest lake in Connecticut and presents diverse opportunities for aquatic ecology. The preserve is predominantly second-growth deciduous and mixed forest, with streams, a large wetland, vernal pools, and small patches of shrubland. More than 4 miles of hiking trails weave through the western half of the preserve and are open to the public year-round. The eastern half of the preserve is closed to the public, but available to staff for research.

Great Hollow conducts conservation-driven studies of biodiversity in Connecticut and beyond to better understand human impacts to the environment and provide science that can help inform management decisions and public policy. Our research spans the fields of animal ecology, ecophysiology, and ecotoxicology as they relate to the effects of invasive species, land-use change, and pollution on wildlife and habitat quality.  We take a collaborative approach to research, working closely with partners across academia, government, and other NGOs to approach questions and conservation issues of common interest. Please browse our website and annual reports for more information on our research.

Great Hollow also operates as a biological field station that is open to external researchers. Facilities at the preserve include seasonal staff housing, offices, a classroom, and a basic wet lab. The lab is modestly equipped with a -80°C freezer, refrigerator, fume hood, research-grade dissecting scope with digital camera, analytical balance, drying oven, autoclave, Soxhlet fat extraction apparatus, Berlese funnels, hemoglobin and hematocrit meter, water bath, microcentrifuges, hematocrit centrifuge, vortexer, variable pipettes, and basic glassware. Applicants should specify whether the research they propose conducting as the Fellow would require any specialized laboratory equipment or analytical capabilities that are not available at Great Hollow (e.g., genetic analyses, isotope analyses). Arrangements can often be made to use, or have samples analyzed in, the labs of other institutions with which Great Hollow collaborates or staff members are affiliated. 

Primary Responsibilities

The Fellow will be responsible for designing and leading ecological research at Great Hollow Nature Preserve and/or other appropriate sites in collaboration with and under the mentorship of Great Hollow’s executive director, Dr. Chad Seewagen. The Fellow will be expected to submit the work for publication within the 24-month fellowship period. Projects that have a clear application to conservation and management are preferred but not required. The Fellow will be expected to apply for extramural funding to help support their research, but their project should be designed to still be feasible if efforts to secure external funding are unsuccessful. A modest internal budget of $2,500 per year for direct research expenses will be provided if external funding is not acquired, and Great Hollow’s summer interns will be available to the Fellow for field assistance.

Apart from their core project, the Fellow will also be responsible for supporting other research projects of Great Hollow’s, including occasional field work and data analysis. The Fellow will be a co-author on any publications that result from projects to which they sufficiently contributed. 

The third primary responsibility of the Fellow will be to help coordinate Great Hollow’s summer internship program along with Great Hollow’s other post-doc and its executive director. This includes helping to manage the internship application and selection process, and mentoring up to two selected interns (who are usually undergraduates, but may sometimes include post-bac or graduate students) as they assist with the Fellow’s project and Great Hollow’s other research projects. The Fellow will be encouraged to use the interns as field assistants in their research and may hire interns with particular skillsets and experience to be most helpful to them.

Secondary Responsibilities

Great Hollow has a small staff, and everyone wears many hats. The Fellow will be expected to be a team player who contributes to the general day-to-day operation of Great Hollow as a member of that small staff. Examples include occasional assistance with education and outreach programs, community events, raptor care, land management, trail maintenance, facilities maintenance, and content creation for Great Hollow’s website, social media, email newsletter, and annual report.

Timeline

The term of the fellowship is 24 months, with minor potential for extension. The start date is somewhat flexible but is preferred to be around March of 2027, assuming the field season for the Fellow’s research would begin around May or June.

Qualifications

PhD in biology, ecology, natural resources, conservation biology, or a related field, preferably earned within the past 5 years. PhD candidates who expect to defend in the spring of 2027 will also be considered if they meet all other criteria.
Independent research experience that includes study design, field work, field-crew supervision, statistical analyses, manuscript preparation and publication of results.
Strong quantitative skills and proficiency with biological statistics, including the use of R and GIS.
Strong scientific writing skills
A minimum of two first-author publications in relevant peer-reviewed journals. Manuscripts in review do not count.
Demonstrated success securing grants or other extramural funding.
Experience presenting at conferences.
Experience teaching or mentoring students.
Familiarity with northeastern U.S. flora, fauna, ecosystems, and general principles of habitat management and environmental conservation.
English fluency and an ability to effectively communicate with other staff, interns, and members of the public both verbally and in writing.
Ability to work well with others as part of a small team in a small working environment.
U.S. citizenship or current authorization to work in the U.S.
Valid driver’s license.

Compensation

The Fellow will receive a compensation package that includes a salary of $60,000 USD per year, employee-only (single-coverage) health insurance, and a year-end, performance-based bonus.

 Application Instructions

Please submit the following to apply

1)    A combined PDF containing:
Cover letter
Curriculum vitae
Research statement (no more than 3 total pages, single-spaced) that includes a description of how your research experience fits the fellowship and Great Hollow’s mission, and brief descriptions of up to three projects that you might propose as the Fellow (~ half page each). Proposed projects are not written in stone and are simply meant to give reviewers a sense of the topics you are most interested in, and your ability to identify project ideas that would be of achievable scope, relevant to the type of research Great Hollow does, and geographically appropriate.
Contact information for, and relationships to, two to three professional references.

2)    PDFs of up to three selected publications.

The deadline to apply is December 15, 2026, but applications will be reviewed as they are received and a selection may be made before then. Applications should be addressed to Great Hollow’s executive director, Chad Seewagen, and emailed to [email removed]. Please put “RESEARCH FELLOWSHIP [Last name_First name]” in the subject line.

Great Hollow is an equal opportunity employer. We are dedicated to providing an inclusive, non-discriminatory and harassment-free environment for all employees, volunteers, members, and program participants. Discrimination or harassment because of age, disability, gender, gender expression, gender identity, nationality, race, religion, sex, sexual orientation, or any other status is not tolerated and is strictly forbidden.

Contact
Chad Seewagen
[email removed] (preferred contact method)

Great Hollow also operates as a biological field station that is open to external researchers. Facilities at the preserve include seasonal staff housing, offices, a classroom, and a basic wet lab. The lab is modestly equipped with a -80°C freezer, refrigerator, fume hood, research-grade dissecting scope with digital camera, analytical balance, drying oven, autoclave, Soxhlet fat extraction apparatus, Berlese funnels, hemoglobin and hematocrit meter, water bath, microcentrifuges, hematocrit centrifuge, vortexer, variable pipettes, and basic glassware. Applicants should specify whether the research they propose conducting as the Fellow would require any specialized laboratory equipment or analytical capabilities that are not available at Great Hollow (e.g., genetic analyses, isotope analyses). Arrangements can often be made to use, or have samples analyzed in, the labs of other institutions with which Great Hollow collaborates or staff members are affiliated. 

Primary Responsibilities

The Fellow will be responsible for designing and leading ecological research at Great Hollow Nature Preserve and/or other appropriate sites in collaboration with and under the mentorship of Great Hollow’s executive director, Dr. Chad Seewagen. The Fellow will be expected to submit the work for publication within the 24-month fellowship period. Projects that have a clear application to conservation and management are preferred but not required. The Fellow will be expected to apply for extramural funding to help support their research, but their project should be designed to still be feasible if efforts to secure external funding are unsuccessful. A modest internal budget of $2,500 per year for direct research expenses will be provided if external funding is not acquired, and Great Hollow’s summer interns will be available to the Fellow for field assistance.

Apart from their core project, the Fellow will also be responsible for supporting other research projects of Great Hollow’s, including occasional field work and data analysis. The Fellow will be a co-author on any publications that result from projects to which they sufficiently contributed. 

The third primary responsibility of the Fellow will be to help coordinate Great Hollow’s summer internship program along with Great Hollow’s other post-doc and its executive director. This includes helping to manage the internship application and selection process, and mentoring up to two selected interns (who are usually undergraduates, but may sometimes include post-bac or graduate students) as they assist with the Fellow’s project and Great Hollow’s other research projects. The Fellow will be encouraged to use the interns as field assistants in their research and may hire interns with particular skillsets and experience to be most helpful to them.

Secondary Responsibilities

Great Hollow has a small staff, and everyone wears many hats. The Fellow will be expected to be a team player who contributes to the general day-to-day operation of Great Hollow as a member of that small staff. Examples include occasional assistance with education and outreach programs, community events, raptor care, land management, trail maintenance, facilities maintenance, and content creation for Great Hollow’s website, social media, email newsletter, and annual report.

Timeline

The term of the fellowship is 24 months, with minor potential for extension. The start date is somewhat flexible but is preferred to be around March of 2027, assuming the field season for the Fellow’s research would begin around May or June.

Qualifications

PhD in biology, ecology, natural resources, conservation biology, or a related field, preferably earned within the past 5 years. PhD candidates who expect to defend in the spring of 2027 will also be considered if they meet all other criteria.
Independent research experience that includes study design, field work, field-crew supervision, statistical analyses, manuscript preparation and publication of results.
Strong quantitative skills and proficiency with biological statistics, including the use of R and GIS.
Strong scientific writing skills
A minimum of two first-author publications in relevant peer-reviewed journals. Manuscripts in review do not count.
Demonstrated success securing grants or other extramural funding.
Experience presenting at conferences.
Experience teaching or mentoring students.
Familiarity with northeastern U.S. flora, fauna, ecosystems, and general principles of habitat management and environmental conservation.
English fluency and an ability to effectively communicate with other staff, interns, and members of the public both verbally and in writing.
Ability to work well with others as part of a small team in a small working environment.
U.S. citizenship or current authorization to work in the U.S.
Valid driver’s license.

Compensation

The Fellow will receive a compensation package that includes a salary of $60,000 USD per year, employee-only (single-coverage) health insurance, and a year-end, performance-based bonus.

 Application Instructions

Please submit the following to apply

1)    A combined PDF containing:
Cover letter
Curriculum vitae
Research statement (no more than 3 total pages, single-spaced) that includes a description of how your research experience fits the fellowship and Great Hollow’s mission, and brief descriptions of up to three projects that you might propose as the Fellow (~ half page each). Proposed projects are not written in stone and are simply meant to give reviewers a sense of the topics you are most interested in, and your ability to identify project ideas that would be of achievable scope, relevant to the type of research Great Hollow does, and geographically appropriate.
Contact information for, and relationships to, two to three professional references.

2)    PDFs of up to three selected publications.

The deadline to apply is December 15, 2026, but applications will be reviewed as they are received and a selection may be made before then. Applications should be addressed to Great Hollow’s executive director, Chad Seewagen, and emailed to [email removed]. Please put “RESEARCH FELLOWSHIP [Last name_First name]” in the subject line.

We are dedicated to providing an inclusive, non-discriminatory and harassment-free environment for all employees, volunteers, members, and program participants. Discrimination or harassment because of age, disability, gender, gender expression, gender identity, nationality, race, religion, sex, sexual orientation, or any other status is not tolerated and is strictly forbidden.

Description:
The Southeastern Cooperative Wildlife Disease Study (SCWDS) and the Warnell School of Forestry and Natural Resources at the University of Georgia (UGA), in close collaboration with the West Virginia Division of Natural Resources (WVDNR), are recruiting a Ph.D. student to lead a comprehensive, field-intensive research program investigating the epidemiological, demographic, and behavioral impacts of sarcoptic mange (Sarcoptes scabiei) on American black bear (Ursus americanus) populations in West Virginia. This project builds upon West Virginia's long-term black bear research foundation to support evidence-based management and to better understand the impacts of sarcoptic mange in black bears.
Key Research Objectives & Scope of Work
·         Longitudinal Disease Tracking and Clinical Evaluations 
·         Mortality and Pathological Assessment
·         Demographic and Reproductive Monitoring
·         Movement Ecology and GPS Telemetry
·         Non-Invasive Camera Trap Arrays and Density Estimation
 Qualifications
We seek a highly motivated, resilient candidate with strong quantitative abilities, excellent field skills, and a commitment to wildlife disease ecology and population management to join a team of graduate students working on the project. 
Minimum Qualifications:
·         Master's degree (M.S.) in Wildlife Biology, Ecology, Wildlife Health, Veterinary Science, or a closely related discipline (exceptional candidates holding a B.S. with extensive research and field leadership experience may be considered). 
·         Minimum cumulative undergraduate/graduate GPA >= 3.0 on a 4.0 scale. 
·         Demonstrated experience conducting wildlife field research, animal capture/handling, and data collection. 
·         Physical capability and willingness to perform strenuous, physically demanding fieldwork in rugged, mountainous terrain under adverse weather conditions.
·         Proficiency and demonstrated aptitude in R programming, spatial analysis (GIS), and quantitative methods in natural resources management. 
·         A valid driver's license and clean driving record.
Preferred Qualifications:
·         Direct experience with chemical immobilization and handling of large mammals, preferably black bears or other carnivores.
·         Experience designing and maintaining remote camera trap grids and analyzing camera data.
·         Prior background in telemetry analysis, movement ecology, spatial statistics, and/or Bayesian hierarchical modeling.
·         Familiarity or interest in learning wildlife diagnostic procedures, necropsy, tissue sampling, parasitology, or health assessments.
·         Proven leadership skills managing field technician crews, coordinating field logistics, and communicating effectively with field team and agency partners. 
·         Demonstrated track record of scientific writing, including peer-reviewed publications and oral presentations. 
 Location & Team Environment
Academic coursework and diagnostic lab work will be based at the University of Georgia in Athens, GA, within the Warnell School of Forestry and Natural Resources and SCWDS. Field research will be conducted across two study regions in West Virginia around Hardy and Pendleton, Pocahontas & Greenbrier counties. The Ph.D. student will join a collaborative, interdisciplinary team of faculty, graduate students, wildlife veterinarians, and agency biologists, working directly with state bear managers. 
 How to Apply
To apply for this graduate assistantship, please compile the following materials into a single PDF document formatted with the file name LastName_FirstName_BearMange_PhD.pdf emailed to all three contacts: 
Cover Letter: A 1–2 page letter describing your research background, quantitative skills, field experience, career goals, and specific interest in this project. 
Curriculum Vitae (CV) / Resume: Highlighting relevant education, research experience, publications, field skills, certifications, and awards. 
Transcripts: Copies of unofficial transcripts for all undergraduate and graduate coursework completed. 
Professional References: Contact information (Name, title, institution, email address, phone number) for three professional or academic references.

Dr. Marcelo Jorge ([email removed])

Dr. Raquel Franscisco ([email removed])
 Application Review: Review of applications will begin immediately, and the position will remain open until a suitable candidate is selected.

Description
The Department of Zoology and Physiology at the University of Wyoming invites applications for the Strickland Family Fish and Wildlife Biometrics Endowed Professorship at the rank of Assistant Professor.  We seek an innovative individual who will develop a collaborative, externally-funded research program that tackles fundamental and applied questions in areas such as hierarchical modeling, statistical study design, population estimation and modeling (e.g., capture-mark-recapture, occupancy, survival) or other quantitatively rigorous area of wildlife and fisheries ecology, or the statistical analyses of complex ecological datasets – with a focus on terrestrial and/or aquatic vertebrates. Importantly, we seek a colleague who moves fluidly between developing new statistical methods, asking fundamental ecological questions, and applying them to pressing wildlife and fisheries management problems or questions at the local (i.e., state of Wyoming), regional, and/or international levels. The successful individual will be expected to contribute to the academic, service, and teaching missions of the Department of Zoology and Physiology, our Wildlife and Fisheries Biology and Management degree, the interdepartmental Ph.D. Program in Ecology and Evolution (PiEE), and more broadly to the University of Wyoming.  Teaching responsibilities may include undergraduate and graduate courses such as ecological statistics, research study design, quantitative methods for wildlife and fisheries (including the development and application of innovative approaches to analyzing ecological data), core courses within the Wildlife and Fisheries Biology and Management major, and/or a new course in the successful applicant’s specialty. The candidate will be expected to participate in appropriate service activities including, but not limited to, serving on departmental, college, and university committees, serving on graduate committees, and providing statistical innovation and support on collaborative grants and research. Candidates are expected to demonstrate a commitment to inclusive, evidence-based teaching and effective mentoring of students from a range of backgrounds and knowledge.   

MINIMUM QUALIFICATIONS: 
PhD in Applied Statistics, Biological or Ecological Statistics, Wildlife or Fisheries Ecology (with clear emphasis on developing innovative statistical methods), or related field
Experience publishing in peer-reviewed journals
Experience or demonstrated interest in teaching undergraduate- and graduate-level courses
Demonstrated history or strong interest in conducting research in one or more of the following areas: hierarchical modeling, statistical study design, or another quantitatively rigorous area of wildlife and fisheries ecology (e.g., population modeling)  

DESIRED QUALIFICATIONS:  
Experience in developing innovative statistical or modeling approaches
Experience collaborating with other researchers or practitioners in the statistical design and analysis elements of data or research
Experience and commitment to excellence in research through multiple first-author publications, including in high-impact journals 
Experience or commitment to effective teaching at the undergraduate and graduate levels
Experience or commitment to effective mentorship of undergraduate and graduate students
Evidence or demonstrated potential to secure external funding
Experience or commitment to engagement with research sponsors, scientists, collaborators, students, or stakeholders representing a spectrum of backgrounds, knowledge, and disciplines 

REQUIRED APPLICATION MATERIALS: 
Complete the online application. Review of applications will begin December 14, 2026; applications received by December 13, 2026 will receive full consideration. In the application, please provide a single PDF file that includes 1) a cover letter (max 2 pages), 2) research statement (max 3 pages), 3) teaching statement (max 2 pages), 4) CV, and 5) contact information for three references. The University of Wyoming conducts background checks on all job candidates upon acceptance of a contingent offer. Questions may be directed to the Search Committee Chair, Dr. Jerod Merkle ([email removed]). Go to the following link for more information and to apply: https://eeik.fa.us2.oraclecloud.com/hcmUI/CandidateExperience/en/sites/CX_1001/job/263005/?utm_medium=jobshare&utm_source=External+Job+Share

Jerod Merkle

The Idaho Department of Fish and Game (IDFG) is seeking qualified candidates for two Regional Wildlife Manager positions. These key leadership opportunities are located in our Panhandle Regional Office in Coeur d’Alene and our Southeast Regional Office in Pocatello, where you will help guide wildlife conservation and management efforts. 

Why IDFG? We are a premier natural resource agency dedicated to preserving, protecting, perpetuating, and managing Idaho's fish and wildlife for this great state. We are committed to creativity, innovation, and excellence as we cultivate opportunities for our customers to engage with our natural resources and become resource stewards for future generations. We are highly dedicated to our mission, committed to our team, and we know how to balance work/life commitments while loving the work we do.

Excellent medical, dental, and vision insurance - employee only coverage for PPO $70.74/month for medical and vision & $12.08/month for dental
